Sun
SūN
n. (rendering Hebrew shemesh and Greek hēlios)
From Old English sunne, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root shared with Latin sōl and Greek hēlios. The Hebrew shemesh is the plain name of the luminary, and it is worth noting what Genesis does not say: in a world where every neighbouring nation named the sun as a god — Shamash in Babylon, Ra in Egypt — Moses declines to name it at all on the fourth day, calling it merely “the greater light to rule the day.” The omission is deliberate polemic. The sun is a lamp, hung by God, and given a job.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The sun is a creature, made on the fourth day, set in the firmament to divide day from night, to rule the day, and to serve for signs and seasons. Scripture's first doctrine of the sun is therefore a demotion: the object the nations worshipped is a servant, and the light it gives was already made on the first day without it. Under this creaturely government it becomes the great figure of God's constancy and impartial common goodness — He “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good” (Mat 5:45), a mercy shed on those who blaspheme Him as freely as on those who bless Him. To Israel the sun is also a figure of God Himself in His giving: “For the LORD God is a sun and shield” (Psa 84:11), light and defence together. The prophetic climax is Mal 4:2, where the Messiah is named the Sun of righteousness arising with healing in his wings — the light that not only shines but heals what it shines on. Ecclesiastes uses the sun differently, as the boundary of the merely natural life: everything done under the sun, considered without reference to God, is vanity, and “there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecc 1:9). Finally, the sun is provisional. In the city of God there is no need of it, for the glory of God lightens it and the Lamb is the light thereof; the lamp is put out when the day it served has fully come.

Webster 1828 Definition

The greater light, made on the fourth day to rule the day and to mark signs and seasons; a creature and never a deity, the emblem of God's constancy and common mercy, of Christ as the Sun of righteousness, and of the bounded natural life in Ecclesiastes.

expand to see more

SUN, n. 1. The splendid orb or luminary which, being in or near the center of our system of worlds, gives light and heat to all the planets.

2. In Scripture, the sun is the greater light appointed to rule the day, and with the moon and stars to be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years. Genesis 1.

3. That which resembles the sun in brightness or in beneficence. The LORD God is a sun and shield. Psalm 84. The Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings. Malachi 4.

4. Under the sun; on the earth; in this present world, considered apart from what is above it. There is no new thing under the sun. Eccles. 1.

5. The worship of the sun was the most ancient and general of the idolatries, and is expressly forbidden in the law, which warns against lifting up the eyes unto the sun and being driven to worship them. Deut. 4.

Key Scripture

Psalm 84:11 — "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."

Malachi 4:2 — "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall."

Ecclesiastes 1:9 — "The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun."

Matthew 5:45 — "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust."

Modern Corruption

The oldest idolatry is sun worship, and its modern form is not a temple but a premise — that the sun and its system are self-explaining, so that the creature that Genesis refuses to name as a god is made the ultimate explanation instead.

expand to see more

The law names this corruption before it happened and forbids it by anticipation: Israel was warned lest they lift up their eyes unto heaven and, seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, be driven to worship and serve them. Ezekiel saw the abomination in the temple itself — five and twenty men with their backs toward the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east, worshipping the sun. Josiah's reformation had to take away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun. This is not a quaint ancient error; it is the permanent instinct of the fallen heart to worship what it can see, and it recurs wherever the visible order is treated as ultimate.

The current form of the error keeps the sun's brightness and drops the Maker. A naturalism that presents the solar system as its own sufficient explanation performs exactly the substitution Rom 1:25 describes — serving the creature more than the Creator — while claiming to have escaped religion altogether. Genesis had already answered it by refusing the sun a name and by making light on the first day, before the lamp existed to carry it. The Christian therefore is free to study the sun as thoroughly as he pleases, and free from any obligation to treat it as ultimate; it is a servant, and it is going out when its work is done.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shemesh is the ordinary name of the luminary, pointedly avoided in the Genesis creation account. Greek hēlios supplies the New Testament term. A separate Hebrew word, chammâh, names the sun poetically as the hot one.

expand to see more

Hebrew shemesh (H8121) — sun; some 134 occurrences. Note its absence from Gen 1:16, where Moses says only “the greater light,” declining the name the nations had deified.

Hebrew chammâh (H2535) — the sun as the hot one, from chāmam, to be warm; the poetic term in Isa 30:26, where the light of the sun shall be sevenfold.

Hebrew 'ōr (H216) — light; made on the first day, before the sun on the fourth, so that light is shewn to be independent of its later vessel.

Greek hēlios (G2246) — sun; used of the sun darkened at the crucifixion (Luk 23:45) and of the face of the Son of man shining as the sun in his strength (Rev 1:16).

Greek anatolē (G395) — a rising, the east, the dayspring; the word of Luk 1:78, “the dayspring from on high hath visited us,” joining the sunrise figure to the incarnation.

Usage

"Of the creature ruling the day: the greater light (Gen 1:16); the sun shall not smite thee by day (Psa 121:6); he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mat 5:45)."

"Of God and of Christ figuratively: the LORD God is a sun and shield (Psa 84:11); the Sun of righteousness with healing in his wings (Mal 4:2); his countenance as the sun shineth (Rev 1:16)."

"Of the bounded natural life in Ecclesiastes: labour under the sun, no new thing under the sun, vanity under the sun — the phrase marking life reckoned without reference to what is above it."
